Verified gains minus all search costs provide delayed credit to sampled edits and work choices, training the Drafter and Policy. Tasks, models, and baselines. We evaluate five scientific domains (PyBaMM, AQM, FDTD, Reactor, and IRP), four system tasks (Terminal-Bench 2.1 (TB2.1), SWE-Pro, GPQA-hard100, and AIME), and separate coding, prompt, and workflow profiles. Qwen3.5-35B-A3B serves as the reference backbone for mechanism studies and the primary matched system comparison. For cross-backbone evaluation on the scientific domains, we additionally test GPT-6-Astra, Claude-Opus-5, Gemini-3.5-Flash, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, GLM-5.3, Kimi-K3, MiniMax-M3, GPT-5.6-Sol, Claude-Sonnet-5-1M, and GPT-5.5, covering 50 backbone–task pairs in total. We further evaluate the four system tasks across twenty model backbones to test whether the observed gains persist across different starting models. Baselines include Janus, HGM, MetaRSI, FlashEvolve, and task-specific optimizers ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Tan et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026b ) . D/H/M permits data, harness, and model edits, whereas D+H excludes model edits. Comparisons remain within matched permission bands; SpecRSI uses direct checks.

Reproducibility. The reference reproduction configuration uses official BF16 Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with a frozen text backbone and rank-16 Drafter LoRA. SFT uses AdamW ( 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} ; component minibatch 1; one epoch); GVO uses two frozen collection/update rounds (group 3; actor/Scorer SGD rates 10 − 3 / 5 × 10 − 4 10^{-3}/5\times 10^{-4} ; at most one joint update per complete collection). Training uses 2,048-token sequences and one H20 per scientific domain; a separate H20 serves 32,768-token inference. Other evaluated backbones use provider APIs. The repository specifies 14 versioned data pools and 42 exact member lists, model/checkpoint identities, simulator parameters, seeds, and separate training/serving software versions.

Artifact controls. Improver updates raise reset/carry gains from 4.1 ± 0.18 4.1\pm 0.18 to 5.2 ± 0.21 5.2\pm 0.21 pp and from 4.8 to 6.2 pp, respectively. Original/updated improvers yield 5.7/6.9 pp from the same released artifact (Table 2 (a)), , showing gains beyond simply retaining a stronger task agent.

SpecRSI’s two-level loop extends incompletely evaluated parents but adopts only complete, admissible versions. VATS allocates edits and complementary checks by predicted net verified return; GVO updates the improver from completed searches under a fixed verification contract. SpecRSI outperforms Janus in all 50 scientific backbone–task pairs and MetaRSI-v1 by 1.85–2.38 pp in four-task macro-average score across twenty backbones. Full planning achieves the highest mean verified gain and lowest total-cost index among tested planning conditions at all eight budget caps. Starting-artifact controls support gains from improver updates beyond retaining stronger task agents. Learned allocation thus turns speculation into verified agent improvement under limited budgets.

This appendix expands Section 4.4 . The experiments progress from controlling the starting artifact, to changing the learned roles and supervision, to running repeated improvement rounds. They test whether the search procedure improves, in addition to the task artifact.

Reset controls return the task agent to the registered starting version while changing the improver. Carry controls retain the stronger task agent. The released-artifact fork is a third comparison: both continuations start from the same already released version, but use original or updated improvers. Comparing across these three starting conditions without holding the starting artifact fixed would conflate learning with artifact retention.

In the reset condition, frozen and all-role-updated improvers obtain 4.1 ± 0.18 4.1\pm 0.18 and 5.2 ± 0.21 5.2\pm 0.21 pp; in the carry condition, they obtain 4.8 ± 0.20 4.8\pm 0.20 and 6.2 ± 0.24 6.2\pm 0.24 pp (Figure S7 a). The difference of update effects is 0.3 pp, but paired runs would be needed for an interaction test.

The earlier acquisition-control record reports reset gain, not the supervision study’s Gain endpoint (Table S14 ). The same-arm means and means-plus-pair rows give 4.8 and 5.3 pp; the extra ordinary-search row gives 4.5 pp.

The multi-round study starts at round 1 and reports rounds 2–5. All four method/improver conditions carry the agent forward; “original” versus “updated” refers to the improver, not whether the task agent is reset. Table 2 (c) gives the raw increments and cumulative gains. For updated SpecRSI, the increments 8.5, 6.4, 4.7, and 2.1 pp accumulate to 21.7 pp. Updated Meta accumulates 17.8 pp, while original-improver SpecRSI accumulates 13.8 pp. Figure S8 separates the gains from improver updates from the differences between methods. Updating the improver raises SpecRSI’s gain in every evaluated round, with cumulative advantages reaching 7.9 pp over its original-improver control and 3.9 pp over updated MetaRSI by round 5. Figure S9 reports seed-level mean increments with task agents carried forward and the real evaluator fixed. Updated SpecRSI leads the other three conditions in every evaluated round across all five training seeds, supporting the consistency of its multi-round advantage.

Reset controls fix the starting task agent while changing the improver checkpoint. They test transfer beyond artifact retention, not improvement of every individual surface or modification of the verification contract Γ \Gamma .

An ordinary Algorithm 1 call initializes the root. A matched continuation instead restores the complete paid state, sets its suffix log empty and clock to zero, fixes ω 0 = a \omega_{0}=a , and enters after the solver. It does not reset the tree, reacquire an already paid menu, or resample the forced first choice. Later decisions use normal paid preparation. Entire forced continuations are excluded from actor updates; they supply critic targets only. The return goes back to the external training caller.

Under serial execution, zero replanning/dispatch cost, no shared setup discounts, identical primitive edits/checks, and a finite primitive allowance, every history-dependent bounded-plan policy can be simulated by a history-dependent singleton policy with identical output and cost distribution.

An executable two-stage adapter supplies a minimal example. An old tool emits an unstructured string consumed by an old parser. Edit e 1 e_{1} changes the output to a structured record; the unchanged parser fails the contract. Edit e 2 e_{2} updates the parser to consume that record. It can then satisfy the contract. This example uses actual transformations and direct executions; it is not a simulated successful observation fed to the drafter. Nor does it show such two-step improvements are common. It explains the distinction between editing permission and adoption permission.
